Verified — the spec's load-bearing claim holds. Ubuntu's `firefox` is `1:1snap1-0ubuntu5`, **epoch 1**, priority 500. An unpinned Mozilla build (`140.x`, no epoch) loses to that on version comparison alone, so adding the Mozilla repo *without* its pin would still install Ubuntu's package. Pins must travel for origin replication to actually work.

Also confirmed the incidental find: `sources.list.d` really does hold `ubuntu.sources.save`, `ubuntu.sources.curtin.orig`, `ubuntu-esm-apps.sources.save` and `ubuntu-esm-infra.sources.save` — four files apt never reads, all currently captured as syncable items because the capture globs `-type f` with no extension filter.

The spec's biggest claim is that **the second mid-`execute()` review can be deleted entirely** — the untested prompt hazard your handover ranks first. Its repo-availability case dissolves because classification now reads the *source's* origins, which no run mutates. Four questions before I brief implementation:

questions.question: Deleting the second review also requires dropping the HELD_OR_PINNED echo (apt_sync.py:352-355, 366-376) — which is separately the cause of the open defect in your handover section 4: a pinned package on the target can never be removed AND its REPORT_ONLY noise can't be silenced. Together that removes ~200 lines, 8 tests, and the mid-apply prompt nothing has ever exercised.

options.label: Delete both (Recommended)
options.description: Drop the HELD_OR_PINNED echo and the second review together. A pin on the target stops suppressing that package's own removal, so the un-removable defect goes away for free. Pins still replicate as files (they must, per the Firefox epoch finding) — what disappears is the per-package echo item reporting that a pin exists, which carries no converge verb and is resolved by fixing the pin anyway.

options.label: Delete the second review, keep the pin echo
options.description: Removes the untested mid-apply prompt but keeps reporting pinned packages. The handover's un-removable-package defect stays open and still needs its own ruling later, and some of the second review's pin-invalidation logic may need to survive in another form.

options.label: Keep both for now
options.description: Smallest diff, but leaves the mid-execute() prompt that has never been rendered by a human or driven by any test — the thing your handover calls the worst gap — in place, plus the open pin defect.

questions.question: ESM on an unattached target: ruling 7 says add esm sources and warn. But writing them to a machine with no Ubuntu Pro attachment likely makes apt-get update fail — and the /etc/apt group is transactional, so that failure would roll back every other repository change in the run.

options.label: Withhold and warn (Recommended, contradicts ruling 7)
options.description: Don't write esm sources to a target with no Pro attachment; warn with the attachment command as remediation. Protects the whole transactional group from one file that cannot work. This is the spec's recommendation and it goes against your literal instruction — flagging that plainly. Note the apt-get-update-fails premise is an unverified hypothesis; I can verify it on a VM before you decide.

options.label: Write and warn, as instructed
options.description: Follow ruling 7 literally: add the esm sources, warn about the missing attachment with remediation. If apt-get update then fails, the transactional group rolls back — losing the run's other repo work — and the user gets a warning plus a failed job. Honest to your stated intent that both machines should have the same sources.

options.label: Write, and exclude esm from the transactional group
options.description: Add them, but don't let an esm failure roll back unrelated repository changes. Keeps ruling 7 intact and contains the blast radius, at the cost of a carve-out in the transaction boundary that ADR-020 currently states absolutely.

questions.question: D-30's collateral prompt currently triggers on the union of BOTH machines' manually-installed sets (apt_sync.py:1628). Your ruling 3 says a follow-up confirmation is asked in exactly one situation — when machine-specific (skip-always) packages on the target are impacted — which is a much narrower trigger.

options.label: Keep D-30's wider trigger (Recommended)
options.description: Leave collateral as-is: ask whenever apt would remove or downgrade a package manually installed on either machine. Ruling 3 was about the new repo-conflict prompt, not about narrowing D-30. Narrowing it means apt can silently remove a package you deliberately installed, just because you never marked it skip-always — which is the exact harm D-30 exists to prevent.

content.text:
Fair challenge — let me correct the framing, because "impacted" was my word and it's misleading.

No apt command ever runs on the source. The source's `apt-mark showmanual` set is already captured as the manifest; D-30 consults it purely as **evidence of your intent**, not as a machine to act on.

The case it covers: apt on the *target* decides it must remove package `Y` to satisfy an approved install. On the target, `Y` is merely an auto-installed dependency — so by the target's own records nobody chose it, and removing it looks harmless. But on the source, `Y` is in `showmanual`: you deliberately installed it there. Since the source is what's being replicated, silently deleting `Y` from the target destroys a package you chose to have — it just happens to have arrived on the target as a dependency rather than by hand. ADR-020 puts it as "the package the user chose on the source but that arrives as collateral on the target."

So the trigger is about *whose intent counts*, not about which machine runs commands. With that correction:

questions.question: Given that correction — the source's manual set is read only as evidence of intent, never acted on — should D-30's collateral prompt keep consulting it? Concretely: apt on the target wants to remove Y to satisfy an approved install; Y is auto-installed on the target but manually installed on the source.

options.label: Keep consulting both sets (Recommended)
options.description: Ask before removing Y. It costs nothing extra at runtime — the source's showmanual set is already captured as the manifest — and it catches the case where a package you deliberately chose on the source gets silently deleted from the target just because it landed there as a dependency. This is today's behaviour and ADR-020's stated reason for it.

options.label: Target's manual set only
options.description: Only ask when Y is manually installed on the TARGET. Simpler rule, and defensible: if the target auto-installed Y, the target's apt owns it. Cost: a package you hand-picked on the source can vanish from the target with no prompt, because the target never recorded it as chosen.

options.label: Skip-always set only, per ruling 3
options.description: Narrowest — ask only when Y is marked machine-specific on the target. One consistent rule for every follow-up prompt in the run. Cost: apt can silently remove manually-installed packages on either machine that were never explicitly marked.

What about pin REMOVAL — a pin deleted on the source, still present on the target?

options.label: Reviewed, two-way like repo removals (Recommended)
options.description: Pin additions and updates always sync silently (they must, or origins don't replicate). Pin REMOVAL gets a review line with remove or skip-once, no registry — the same shape you chose for repositories. Deleting a pin is destructive: it can flip which vendor's package the target installs on the next upgrade.

options.description: Pins mirror the source completely and silently, in both directions. Simplest and most predictable — /etc/apt/preferences.d just matches. But a pin deletion can silently change which vendor supplies a package on the target's next upgrade, with nothing shown.

options.description: Consistent with the choice you just made for apt.conf.d: pins get review lines for add, change and remove. But it means an approved package whose origin needs a pin could have that pin left unticked — reintroducing exactly the "package ticked, its source unticked" inconsistency that derived repos exist to make unrepresentable.

All rulings are in. The model is fully specified. Two consequences worth naming: **D-30 is narrowed** (collateral now consults the target's manual set only — the source-intent case is deliberately given up), and **apt.conf.d keeps review lines**, so "only packages are reviewed" is a near-rule rather than an absolute.

DOC task in /home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher, branch `gsd/phase-02-package-management-sync`. Update one spec and write one new ADR. DO NOT change any source file. DO NOT commit. DO NOT push. Do not touch the pc1/pc2 VMs or the Hetzner lock. Read-only shell commands only.

## Context

Read `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-SPEC-package-review-model.md` — you (or a predecessor) wrote it. The user has now answered every open question in its section 11, plus two follow-ups. Your job is to fold those answers in so the spec is final and implementation-ready, then write the ADR that supersedes ADR-020.

Also read: `docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md`, `docs/adr/adr-001-adr.md` (the ADR process and the immutability rule at `:15`), `docs/adr/_index.md` (for the next free ADR number and the index format).

## The final rulings — all decided, none open

Carrying forward from the spec as written:
1. Review shows packages, each naming its origin when that origin is not the distribution archive, in full-URI-path form (`ppa.launchpadcontent.net/git-core/ppa/ubuntu/`, not just the host).
2. Repository ADD is derived from approved packages; never a tickable line.
3. Repository REMOVAL is reviewed, two answers only — remove or skip-once. No registry entry, no skip-always.
4. Repository CHANGE overwrites the target silently, EXCEPT when a machine-specific (target skip-always) package comes from that file: then show both file contents and ask overwrite or skip-once.
5. `ubuntu.sources`, `/etc/apt/sources.list` and `ubuntu-esm-*` are never REMOVED, but are written and updated.
6. Origin replication is enforced by a batched `apt-cache policy` on the target AFTER `apt-get update` and BEFORE the first install: the candidate's origins must intersect the source's, or the item fails.
7. Pins must travel — verified on the dev machine: Ubuntu's `firefox` candidate is `1:1snap1-0ubuntu5`, epoch 1 at priority 500, so an unpinned vendor version loses on version comparison and adding the vendor repo alone would still install Ubuntu's package.
8. `sources.list.d` capture is filtered to `*.list` and `*.sources` — verified present on the dev machine and currently captured as syncable items: `ubuntu.sources.save`, `ubuntu.sources.curtin.orig`, `ubuntu-esm-apps.sources.save`, `ubuntu-esm-infra.sources.save`. `preferences.d` keeps no extension filter; it legitimately holds extensionless files.
9. Packages keep their three-way decision and machine-local registry (ADR-020 D-07/D-08 intact). CONFIRMED by the user, no longer an assumption.
10. No backwards compatibility anywhere. No migration code, no legacy-entry reading, no shims. There are no existing `apt:source:` decision records.
11. Long CLI options in every command string.
12. Bare-`.deb` packages are `manual_installs_sync`'s exclusive territory (shipped in `30a9eb6f`).

NEW answers to fold in — these change the spec:
13. **Delete the second mid-`execute()` review AND the `HELD_OR_PINNED` echo together** (`apt_sync.py:352-355, 366-376`, and `089ea985`'s `_rereview_repo_invalidated_packages`). This also closes the open defect at `02-HANDOVER-package-review.md:62` — a pinned package on the target could never be removed and its `REPORT_ONLY` noise could never be silenced. Pins still replicate as FILES; what goes is the per-package echo item reporting that a pin exists.
14. **ESM: withhold and warn.** Do NOT write `ubuntu-esm-*` sources to a target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment; warn, with the attachment command as copy-paste remediation. This deliberately contradicts the literal reading of ruling 5 and the user knows it — the reason is that the `/etc/apt` group is transactional, so an `apt-get update` failure from an unusable ESM source would roll back every other repository change in the run. The premise that an unattached ESM source makes `apt-get update` fail is an UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESIS — mark it as such in the spec and say what would settle it (a VM test).
15. **D-30 collateral narrows to the TARGET's manual set only.** Today it triggers on the union of both machines' manual sets (`apt_sync.py:1628`). The source-intent case — a package manually installed on the source that arrives on the target as an auto dependency and gets removed as collateral — is deliberately given up. Record it as a knowingly accepted loss with its rationale ("if the target auto-installed it, the target's apt owns it"), not as an oversight. This OVERTURNS part of ADR-020 D-30.
16. **`/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` stays reviewed in both directions** — add, change and remove all get review lines. Consequence to state plainly: "only packages are reviewed" is therefore a near-rule, not an absolute; apt config is the deliberate exception because nothing about an approved package implies whether an apt config file should travel.
17. **Pins: adds and updates always sync silently; pin REMOVAL is reviewed two-way** (remove or skip-once, no registry) — the same shape as repository removal, because deleting a pin can flip which vendor supplies a package on the target's next upgrade.

- Re-check the staged implementation plan (section 9) and the test plan (section 10) against all of it. The staging must still end each stage green.

## Deliverable 2 — the superseding ADR

`docs/adr/adr-001-adr.md:15` makes accepted ADRs immutable: they are superseded, not edited. ADR-020 is `Status: Accepted`. Write the new ADR at `docs/adr/adr-0NN-<slug>.md` using the next free number from `docs/adr/_index.md`, following ADR-001's required structure and the house format of the existing ADRs (read two or three recent ones to match register and section order).

- State clearly which ADR-020 decisions it OVERTURNS (at minimum: D-07's "every actionable item gets a three-way decision" now has documented exceptions; D-11's "apt sources are inventory items" in the add direction; D-30's collateral trigger; the D-24 second-review allowance that ruling 13 removes) and which it CARRIES FORWARD UNCHANGED (D-01, D-02, D-03, D-15, D-16, D-18, D-29 and the rest — enumerate them, do not hand-wave).

- Update `docs/adr/_index.md` with the new entry, and mark ADR-020's index entry as superseded by it. Check how the index represents superseded ADRs before inventing a convention; if there is no precedent, mirror whatever ADR-020's own header does and say what you chose.
- Do NOT edit the body of ADR-020 itself beyond whatever status/superseded-by header the project's own convention requires. If the convention is unclear, say so in your report rather than guessing.

## Style rules
Terse. No `---` separators. No bold-as-heading — real heading levels only. No hard-wrapping mid-sentence (one paragraph = one line). Cite `path:line` for claims about code. Label unverified reasoning as hypothesis. Prose specs and exact signatures, never ready-made implementations, and do not paste existing source into either document.

content.subject: Fix the apt no-candidate detector
content.description: _packages_with_no_candidate tests for literal "Candidate: (none)" which apt does not print for hand-installed .debs. Replace with the dpkg-status-only-origin test (reuse _installed_origins_by_package). Copies in manual_installs_sync.py and apt_sync.py. Needs analysis of which call site needs which predicate, then fix + RED-proven tests.

content.subject: Derive apt repo additions from approved packages
content.description: apt sources stop being independently reviewable items for ADD. Adding a repo is derived from packages approved from it; repo named in the package's review detail; removal stays reviewed; /etc/apt/sources.list and ubuntu.sources are NEVER collected. Follow d27337da (keys) for shape, 43a52fa3 for detail naming. Update 02-SCENARIO-COVERAGE.md C-section rows and docs.
content.activeForm: Deriving repo additions from approved packages

content.subject: Prepare UAT test 1 for the human-driven review
content.description: The batched review has never been driven by a human. Produce copy-paste commands for the user to run 02-UAT.md test 1 themselves, covering questionary checkbox render, Rich Live pause/resume, second mid-execute review (089ea985, apt_sync.py:1410-1441), multi-line snippet editor, collateral prompt, Ctrl-C/EOF abort. Do not drive it.

content.subject: Fix name-only package matching (Firefox danger)
content.description: apt_sync matches packages by name only, so a source package from a vendor repo can be silently installed from Ubuntu's archive on the target. Replicate origin: the review shows the package's source when not Ubuntu, and apt_sync does whatever is needed (repo+key+pin) to install from that same origin. Folded into task 2.

content.subject: Supersede ADR-020 with the revised review model
content.description: ADR-001 makes accepted ADRs immutable, so ADR-020 must be superseded, not edited. Changes: only packages are reviewed with three-way decisions; repo add is derived; repo removal is two-way (remove/skip-once, no registry); repo change overwrites unless machine-specific packages are affected; ubuntu.sources/esm never removed but updated/added; origin is part of package identity.

**ADR-021 is written and ADR-020 superseded** — committed in `b940f804`, along with the spec and the UAT runbook.

`ADR-021: Origin-replicating package convergence — the review decides packages, /etc/apt follows`. New decisions D-34 through D-40. It follows the existing ADR-016→017 supersession convention rather than inventing one, and leaves ADR-020's body untouched.

What it overturns: D-02's *enumeration* (sources and pins stop being items for add/change), D-07's universality (two-answer exceptions now exist), D-11/D-13's inventory model in the add/change direction, D-24's "MAY review again" clause, D-25's taxonomy (`HELD_OR_PINNED` retired, `REPO_UNAVAILABLE` redefined, `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` added), and D-30's trigger. Carried forward unchanged and enumerated: D-01, D-03–D-06, D-08–D-10, D-12, D-15–D-23, D-26–D-29, D-33.

The agent pushed back on one premise in my brief and was right: I'd listed D-02 as carried forward while the spec listed it as overturned. Both are true of different halves — D-02's *principle* ("mechanism the user has no basis to judge is not an item") is the clause that licenses this whole change, so it carries forward; only its enumeration narrows. attachment.snippet:
1	# Package Sync
2	
3	The package jobs replicate *what is installed* — apt packages plus the `/etc/apt` repository configuration they depend on, snaps, flatpaks, and the things no package manager can reproduce — rather than user data. Package *data* (`~/.var/app`, `~/snap/<app>/common`, dotfiles) stays `folder_sync`'s territory. The package sync jobs are about the presence, version and provenance of the packages themselves.
4	
5	Configuration for these jobs is limited to their `sync_jobs` enable flags; see the [configuration reference](../configuration.md#sync_jobs). There are no per-job config keys.
6	
7	## The four jobs
8	
9	Four independent jobs share one item -> diff -> review -> converge model. Each has its own enable flag, its own validation, its own review and its own failure isolation, so enabling one never drags in another.
10	
11	```yaml
12	sync_jobs:
13	  apt_sync: false             # apt packages plus the /etc/apt repository configuration they depend on
14	  snap_sync: false            # installed snaps, converged to the source's revision and channel
15	  flatpak_sync: false         # installed flatpak refs and their remotes, per scope
16	  manual_installs_sync: false # things no package manager can reproduce, plus the install-snippet registry
17	```
18	
19	All four ship **disabled**: enabling any of them lets pc-switcher change installed software on the target, so it is opt-in.
20	
21	### What each job covers
22	
23	- **`apt_sync`** — the manually-installed apt package set (`apt-mark showmanual`, not the full dpkg selection — apt resolves dependencies on the target itself), minus the packages you installed from a hand-downloaded `.deb` (see below), plus the repository configuration that governs where packages come from: sources under `/etc/apt/sources.list.d`, pins (`/etc/apt/preferences.d`) and apt config (`/etc/apt/apt.conf.d`). Signing keys travel too, but you are never asked about them — see [Signing keys](#signing-keys).
24	- **`snap_sync`** — installed snaps, converged to the source's exact revision and tracking channel.
25	- **`flatpak_sync`** — installed flatpak refs and their remotes, per user/system installation scope.
26	- **`manual_installs_sync`** — everything no package manager can reproduce: apt packages installed from no configured repository (a `.deb` you installed by hand), plus unowned files under `/usr/local` and `/opt`. It also owns the [install-snippet registry](#install-snippets).
27	
28	### Hand-installed `.deb` packages belong to one job only
29	
30	A package whose installed version comes from no repository your machine has configured was put there with `dpkg --install`. It is `manual_installs_sync`'s territory exclusively: `apt_sync` detects the same packages, with the same test, and drops them from its manifest before it diffs anything. They produce no apt item, no review entry and no install.
31	
32	There is nothing apt could do with them anyway. The target's apt has never heard the name, so offering it as an ordinary install would fail with "Unable to locate package" — while `manual_installs_sync` offers the same package as an [install snippet](#install-snippets) in the same run. Only one of the two answers works, so only one job asks.
33	
34	The consequence is worth knowing: the two jobs have separate enable flags, and `apt_sync` does not consult `manual_installs_sync`'s. **If you enable `apt_sync` but disable `manual_installs_sync`, your hand-installed `.deb` packages are synced by nobody** — they are silently absent from the review rather than offered as installs that fail. Keep `manual_installs_sync` enabled if you install software from downloaded `.deb` files.
35	
36	## Job ordering is enforced
37	
38	The three package-manager jobs **must** be listed before `folder_sync` in `sync_jobs`. This is not a convention: pc-switcher validates the order and aborts the run with a config error if any of `apt_sync`, `snap_sync` or `flatpak_sync` is enabled but sits after `folder_sync` (`orchestrator._check_package_jobs_precede_folder_sync`).
39	
40	The reason is the "defaults, then your data" layering. Installing software usually writes its own default config and data files on first appearance. If `folder_sync` ran first, the target would have your synced versions of those files, and then the fresh install would overwrite them with stock defaults. Running the package jobs first means the software (and its defaults) already exists when `folder_sync` lands your versions on top — so your tweaks win, not the installer's defaults.
41	
42	## Batched review
43	
44	Because an enabled package job can install or remove software on the target, each one shows you a review and waits for your approval before it changes anything.
45	
46	The review lists every difference the job found between source and target, grouped by action, and installs are always kept separate from removals: a group that would install software is never mixed with one that would remove it, and a removal group names the removal explicitly (for example "Remove packages") rather than saying "apply". Removal groups start **unticked**, so a bulk approval can never silently delete something.
47	
48	Every item that would actually change something — an install, a removal, or a change to match the source, holds and masks included — offers the same three-way choice:
49	
50	- **Apply** it — make this change on the target.
51	- **Skip this run** — leave it alone for now; it comes back next sync.
52	- **Skip always** — mark it as belonging to this machine only, so no future sync touches it (see [Machine-specific packages](#machine-specific-packages)).
53	
54	You give those answers with two lists per group, not with a question per item. The first list is the apply list: ticked means apply. Whatever you leave unticked is then offered once more — "never offer again on this machine?" — and ticking it there is skip-always. Ticking nothing on that second list (just pressing Enter) is skip-this-run, so the items come back next sync. If you ticked everything for apply, the second list is not shown at all. Ctrl-C at either list aborts the whole sync.
55	
56	Items that only **report** a condition are not offered skip-always: a version difference between source and target, an apt package the target's own repositories offer no candidate for, and the pin echo on a held or pinned package. These change nothing on the target, and neither machine "holds" the item in the way a machine-specific mark requires — marking a version difference would silently stop the package syncing altogether rather than stop reporting the drift. Resolve them by fixing the underlying condition (align the versions, add the repository, remove the pin).
57	
58	### A second apt review, when this run changed `/etc/apt`
59	
60	`apt_sync` reads the target's pins and asks its apt what it can install while it builds the review — and then, in the same run, rewrites `/etc/apt`. Both of those facts can be false by the time packages are converged: a pin you just deleted was still suppressing its packages when the list was drawn, and a repository you just installed can supply a package apt had no candidate for.
61	
62	So `apt_sync` converges the repository configuration first, re-reads the target it has just produced, and — if that genuinely changed anything — shows you one more screen with what it revealed. Its groups are marked "(revealed by this run's /etc/apt changes)". Everything you already answered stands; only the newly-actionable items are asked about. Approvals the new state contradicts go the other way and are simply dropped: if a pin file you installed now governs a package you had approved for removal, that removal is abandoned without another question.
63	
64	A run that changes nothing under `/etc/apt` never shows a second screen, and neither does a dry run — nothing is written, so nothing is invalidated. A dry-run preview therefore shows the pre-repository classification of packages, which is the one place this staleness is still visible.
65	
66	### Confirming every individual command
67
